stories.headline: Flood fury in AP as rivers swell
stories.title: Flood fury in AP as rivers swell
stories.summary: Flood warnings issued as Vamsadhara, Nagavali swell
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: Following heavy rains over the past four days triggered by the severe depression that crossed the state coast, Andhra Pradesh remained on high flood alert on Friday as the continual downpour sent large volumes of water into rivers, reservoirs, and barrages.
The latest reservoir data showed substantial inflows into several projects, with authorities releasing much of the incoming water downstream to maintain storage levels and regulate flood flows.
The impact was particularly pronounced in Srikakulam, where the Vamsadhara and Nagavali rivers continued to swell following heavy rainfall in the district and upstream areas of Odisha.
A first danger warning remained in force at Gotta Barrage, where the latest reservoir data showed an inflow of 44,900 cusecs and outflow of 45,679 cusecs.
At Narayanapuram Anicut, inflow and outflow were both around 66,900 cusecs, with officials maintaining a close watch on the rising flood levels.
Residents in low-lying and riverbank areas have been advised to remain alert.
The Nagavali was also receiving heavy flows from the upstream catchment, besides water released from Thotapalli and Madduvalasa projects.
Thotapalli recorded 23,250 cusecs each of inflow and outflow, while Madduvalasa received 25,100 cusecs and released 26,000 cusecs.
Flood waters have begun entering agricultural fields in villages in Burja and Amadalavalasa mandals.
The Prakasam Barrage in Vijayawada was also receiving a major surge, with 40,521 cusecs of inflow and an equal quantity being released downstream.
Flood waters from the Munneru, Kattaleru and Budameru streams contributed to the sharp rise, prompting the opening of 20 gates.
This was the first major surplus release from the barrage this season.

stories.headline: Congress hopes for calm in Punjab unit but storm clouds remain ahead of 2027 Assembly election
stories.title: Congress hopes for calm in Punjab unit but storm clouds remain ahead of 2027 Assembly election
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The absence of a few senior leaders, including former Chief Minister Charanjit Singh Channi, from the Punjab Congress unit’s demonstration on Friday in Chandigarh against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar has again raised questions about the party’s internal cohesion.
The July 1 revamp of the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) had sparked turmoil in the Punjab unit.

Amarinder Singh Raja Warring was retained as the PPCC chief, and Mr. Channi, the Lok Sabha member from Jalandhar and the Congress’s most prominent Dalit face in the State, was appointed to lead the election campaign committee in the run-up to the 2027 Assembly election.
Mr. Channi and a few other leaders, including Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, Rana Gurjit and Tript Rajinder Singh Bajwa, were believed to be upset with the revamp of the party unit.
Their supporters demanded that Mr. Warring be replaced as PPCC president, exposing the factional fault lines within the State unit.

With the elections approaching and differences persisting, the central leadership of the Congress brought in Sachin Pilot to replace Bhupesh Baghel, a former Chhattisgarh Chief Minister, as the general secretary in charge of the poll-bound State.
Soon after taking charge, Mr. Pilot asserted that nearly all the leaders in Punjab have assured him of working collectively and unitedly.

Amid the ongoing power tussle, particularly between Mr. Channi and the PPCC president, the senior leaders showed a rare sign of unity by participating in the demonstration on September 9 against the Punjab government in Chandigarh, led by Mr. Pilot, a former Rajasthan Deputy Chief Minister.

A party source said earlier this week that a meeting regarding the State unit took place at the residence of national president Mallikarjun Kharge, where senior party leader Rahul Gandhi and Mr. Pilot were present.
Mr. Pilot reportedly submitted a detailed feedback report on the affairs of the Punjab unit to the party’s top leadership.
The source added, “The situation in the State unit at present is quiet, but it could be like a calm before the storm.
The party high command had asked the new in-charge to take a broad view of the PPCC’s affairs and issues and share it.

stories.headline: Election Commission must respond to SIR irregularity allegations, says Ram Madhav
stories.title: Election Commission must respond to SIR irregularity allegations, says Ram Madhav
stories.summary: BJP leader says Opposition should not contest elections if it believes the electoral system is rigged
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national vice-president V. Ram Madhav said on Friday that the Election Commission of India (ECI) would have to respond to allegations of large-scale irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
He also indicated that Narendra Modi would remain the BJP’s prime ministerial candidate, saying that Mr. Modi would win two or three more elections.

Addressing a memorial lecture, ‘Ism Nee Payanam Etu’, after releasing the book Jaateeya Bhavam Karuvaina Communistlu here, Mr. Ram Madhav said the Congress and other Opposition parties should decide whether their victories in Kerala, Karnataka and Telangana were achieved because of “crumbs” from the BJP.
He said the Opposition should not contest elections if it genuinely believed that the electoral system was rigged.
In an apparent reference to Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders Abhijit Dipke and others, Mr. Ram Madhav said some young leaders were emerging but lacked political maturity.

He said they were advising Opposition parties to stay away from what they described as “fixed matches” and “rigged elections”, while claiming that the Opposition had secured small, isolated victories with the BJP’s support.
“Is it so?” he asked the Opposition parties.
Mr. Ram Madhav also criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and questioned how he had concluded that the ECI was helping the BJP win elections.
If that were the case, he said, the ECI constituted by the Congress before 2014 was in place when elections were held in 2014, 2015 and 2016.

Responding to criticism of Mr. Modi’s electoral victories, he said that if the Prime Minister had won three elections without popular support, it was pertinent to recall that Jawaharlal Nehru had also won three elections.
Mr. Modi would win more elections because of his commitment and dedication to uplifting the last person in society, or Antyodaya, he said.

Mr. Ram Madhav said the concept of Antyodaya, articulated by Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya to ensure that the benefits of development reached the last person in society, was reflected in the welfare programmes of the Narendra Modi government.

stories.headline: Chirag and Upendra Kushwaha ask Election Commission to dispel confusion in minds of the people
stories.title: Chirag and Upendra Kushwaha ask Election Commission to dispel confusion in minds of the people
stories.summary: Union Minister and LJP(RV) leader says if questions are being raised about the Commission, then it is the responsibility of the Commission, and specifically Gyanesh Kumar, to strongly present his own side
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Bharatiya Janata Party felt the heat within its alliance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise on Friday, as Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) leader Chirag Paswan and Rashtriya Lok Morcha (RLM) leader Upendra Kushwaha urged the Election Commission of India (EC) to dispel confusion in the minds of the people.

Both Bihar leaders issued statements amid the demand of the Congress that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign immediately after an Indian Express report claimed that two of the three Election Commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally recorded objections at least 14 times over the last 10 months.
He further said, “The Commission should present its position strongly to the people, and that is the beauty of democracy.
If people lose confidence in the election process or if doubts arise, then it’s wrong.
I feel the Commission should present its side.
This is not to respond to Rahul Gandhi or the Opposition, but to ensure that no doubts remain in the minds of the people.”
Earlier this week, Leader of the Opposition in the Bihar Assembly Tejashwi Yadav had said reports had revealed how the BJP intends to dismantle the Constitution and democracy.
He had even asked why there was silence over the questions raised by the two Election Commissioners.
Mr. Yadav had further urged Mr. Kumar to come forward and respond to the allegations.
Mr. Kushwaha echoed the comments in a post on X. “A lot of confusion has arisen among the people over the controversy related to the SIR.
The matter needs to be addressed.
To dispel the confusion, the Election Commission should immediately come out with the clarification.”

stories.headline: NDA allies ask Election Commission to clear air on internal differences over SIR
stories.title: NDA allies ask Election Commission to clear air on internal differences over SIR
stories.summary: Opposition begins protest after the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, demanded the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Two NDA allies, Lok Janshakti Party leader and Union Minister of Food Processing Industries Chirag Paswan and Rashtriya Lok Morcha leader Upendra Kushwaha, on Friday joined the debate on Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s conduct, asking the Election Commission of India to “dispel misgivings in the minds of the people” arising out of reports of alleged internal differences within the poll panel over Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Though the BJP came out to defend the Election Commission of India and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, who is at the centre of controversy, Paswan stressed in Patna that “as part of the government,” he did not intend to “defend a Constitutional body”.
“Let me make it clear that, as part of the government, I do not intend to defend a constitutional body.
I am also not very worried about the allegations made by the opposition, which will always take a stand that suits it politically,” the Union Minister told reporters.

As per the news reports, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi wrote 14 times in ten days about the deletion and addition of voters to the electoral roll, as well as on other issues.
“If the people start losing trust in the electoral system, that will not augur well for democracy.
Therefore, I think the Election Commission must come out with its clarification more forcefully.
It need not respond to what Rahul Gandhi and his associates are saying, but it must dispel the misgivings in the minds of the people,” said the Hajipur MP.
Upendra Kushwaha, who is also a Rajya Sabha MP, said on X: “There is a lot of confusion among the public about SIR.
This issue needs to be addressed.
Election Commission has to clarify this without delay.”

Meanwhile, the opposition continued with its protest after the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, demanded the resignation of CEC Kumar and charged that recent elections have been rigged by the Commission.

stories.headline: Supreme Court reserves verdict on Sambhal Mosque Committee's plea against survey
stories.title: Supreme Court reserves verdict on Sambhal Mosque Committee's plea against survey
stories.summary: Supreme Court reserves verdict on Sambhal Mosque Committee's plea against survey
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: 2 independent source groups -> high confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday reserved its judgment on the plea filed by the Sambhal Jama Masjid Committee challenging the Allahabad High Court's order which upheld the trial court's order to appoint an advocate commissioner to survey the mosque in a suit filed by Hindu plaintiffs.

A bench comprising Justice PS Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe heard arguments from Senior Advocate Huzefa Ahmadi and Advocate Nizam Pasha for the mosque committee, Advocate Hari Shankar Jain for the Hindu plaintiffs and Additional Solicitor General KM Nataraj for the State of Uttar Pradesh.

The dispute arises from a civil suit filed by Hindu plaintiffs in 2024 seeking the right to access the Sambhal Jama Masjid for performing religious ceremonies on the claim that it was originally a Hindu temple which was demolished in the 16th century to build a mosque.
The trial court had appointed an Advocate Commissioner to conduct a local investigation of the mosque premises on November 19, 2024.
The Allahabad High Court, in its May 19, 2025 order, upheld the survey order and held that the suit cannot be held to be barred by the Places of Worship Act at this stage.
The mosque committee had raised its main arguments on the previous dates, and today, the plaintiffs and the State responded, with the mosque committee making rejoinder arguments at the end.
ASG KM Nataraj, appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh, told the Court that the State did not wish to enter into the merits of the dispute since the main suit was pending trial.

"I don't want to get into the merits because the main matter is not pending before the court," Nataraj submitted, adding that the State was bound to protect the interests of both sides since the dispute concerned religious rights.
His submissions, however, focused on the interpretation of the Places of Worship Act.

Referring to Sections 2 and 3 of the Act, Nataraj submitted that Section 2 defines "conversion" to include alteration or changes, while Section 3 imposes a prohibition on conversion of a place of worship.

He pointed out that the expression "place of worship" is defined broadly and argued that the question whether a particular proceeding is barred would depend upon whether it concerns conversion of the religious character of the place.

Nataraj also referred to the provisions concerning religious denominations and Article 26 of the Constitution, submitting that the expression "religious denomination" may have to be considered in the context of the entire religion or a section thereof.

stories.title: YSRCP chief Jagan seeks amendment to CEC appointment law
stories.summary: YSRCP chief YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has urged the Centre to amend the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, and restore the earlier appointment system involving the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice of India.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: YSRCP chief YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has urged the Centre to amend the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, and restore the earlier appointment system involving the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition and Chief Justice of India.

Amaravati: Former Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister and YSR Congress Party President YS Jagan Mohan Reddy on Friday demanded an amendment to the CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, to restore public confidence in the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and other Election Commissioners.

He called for a return to the earlier system under which the CEC and other Election Commissioners were appointed by a three-member committee comprising the Leader of Opposition (LoP), the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the Prime Minister.

In his first reaction to the ongoing row involving CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Jagan said in a post on X that democracy can stand only when people have complete confidence in constitutional institutions such as the Election Commission.

“National media reports that two Election Commissioners raised objections on several occasions to decisions, electoral rolls, and the management of ECINet, which have led to serious questions and doubts among the public.

Rather than an exchange of allegations, the public needs clarity on what objections were recorded, what action was taken on them, and how transparently the system functioned, whether for adding, deleting, or restoring names on electoral rolls.
Steps are needed to give people confidence on these matters,” he said.
He added that public trust in the electoral process must be strengthened, every citizen’s right to vote protected, and systems reinforced to allow people to exercise that right without fear.
“In a democracy, transparency should not only prevail but should also appear to have prevailed.

The very bill (Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023), which we supported then, should be revisited now in the current context.
The Central government should come forward, set the norm in place, and dispel this fear.
An amendment to the bill should be brought forward where the Election Commissioner is appointed by the three-member committee of LoP, CJI and the Prime Minister once again,” the YSRCP said.

stories.headline: Climate Change and Kashmir
stories.title: Climate Change and Kashmir
stories.summary: Kashmir has always been described through its seasons. Spring arrives with almond blossoms and soft sunlight. Summer brings green meadows, clear streams and the cool comfort of the mountains. Autumn paints the valley in gold, while winter covers its roofs and fields with snow. This changing rhythm has shaped the culture, economy and imagination of the people. But that rhythm is no longer as reliable as it once was. The signs of climate change are now visible in the valley’s everyday life. Winters are becoming shorter and less predictable. Snowfall patterns have changed. Summers are hotter, water sources are under pressure, and sudden rainfall often turns into flooding. Glaciers are shrinking, forests are facing greater stress, and agriculture is becoming more difficult to plan. Climate change is no longer an abstract phrase used in international conferences. It is present in the drying spring, the failing crop, the unusual snowfall and the anxious farmer looking at the sky. Kashmir is often presented as a paradise, but paradise is not immune to environmental damage. In fact, its beauty can sometimes hide its vulnerability. The same mountains, lakes and forests that attract visitors also sustain local communities. When they are weakened, the consequences are not limited to the landscape. They affect livelihoods, public health, food security and the future of generations yet to be born. The most visible impact of climate change in Kashmir is perhaps the disturbance of winter. Snow has never been merely a scenic part of the valley’s identity. It is a vital source of water. Snow stored in the mountains gradually feeds rivers, streams and springs as temperatures rise. It supports agriculture, replenishes groundwater and maintains the flow of rivers during the warmer months. When snowfall is delayed, reduced or concentrated into short and intense periods, the entire water cycle is disturbed. Farmers face uncertainty over irrigation. Hydropower projects may experience fluctuations. Villages dependent on springs find their traditional water sources weakening. The problem becomes more serious when warmer temperatures cause snow to melt too quickly, leaving less water available later in the season. The changing climate is also affecting agriculture, one of the main foundations of Kashmir’s rural economy. The timing of apple blossoms, pollination and harvesting is increasingly vulnerable to sudden changes in temperature. An unusually warm spell followed by frost can damage blossoms and reduce production. Hailstorms, untimely rain and heat stress can affect fruit quality. Farmers who once relied on familiar seasonal patterns now have to make decisions in conditions they cannot easily predict. The apple industry provides an important example. Kashmir’s horticulture sector supports thousands of families directly and many more indirectly. It contributes to transport, packaging, storage, trade and employment. Yet the sector is exposed to rising temperatures, changing chill hours, water scarcity and extreme weather. If climate change continues without effective adaptation, the impact will be felt far beyond orchards. It will reach markets, workers, transporters and consumers. Paddy cultivation is also under pressure. Agriculture in Kashmir depends heavily on water availability and a predictable monsoon. Erratic rainfall can create both drought-like conditions and damaging floods. A farmer may face a shortage of water at one stage of cultivation and excessive rain at another. This makes traditional knowledge less dependable and increases financial risk for small and marginal farmers. Climate change is not only an environmental crisis. It is also a social justice issue. Those who have contributed least to global warming often suffer the most from its effects. A small farmer cannot control industrial emissions, global energy policies or the decisions of large corporations. Yet the farmer bears the cost when crops fail, water sources dry up or extreme weather destroys an orchard. Similarly, a poor household cannot easily adapt to rising temperatures. It may not have reliable heating, cooling, insulation or access to healthcare. Families living in vulnerable areas face greater risks from floods and landslides. Women, children, the elderly and people with disabilities are often affected disproportionately during environmental emergencies, even though their concerns receive limited attention in planning and policy. The valley’s water bodies provide another warning. Dal Lake, Wular Lake and other wetlands are not simply tourist attractions. They are ecological systems that regulate water, support biodiversity and protect communities from flooding. Encroachment, pollution, excessive construction and untreated waste have already weakened many of these water bodies. Climate change adds another layer of pressure. When intense rainfall occurs, degraded wetlands cannot absorb and hold water as effectively as healthy ecosystems. The result is greater flooding in urban and rural areas. At the same time, warmer temperatures can encourage the growth of weeds and harmful organisms in lakes, reducing water quality and threatening aquatic life. The destruction of wetlands, therefore, is not only a loss of natural beauty. It is a direct threat to public safety. Urbanisation has made the situation more complicated. Srinagar and other towns are expanding rapidly, often without adequate attention to drainage, land use and ecological limits. Buildings are coming up in areas that once absorbed rainwater. Roads and concrete surfaces prevent water from entering the soil. Drains are frequently blocked by waste, while construction continues along water channels and wetlands. A changing climate exposes the weaknesses of such development. Even a moderate spell of heavy rain can create serious disruption when natural drainage systems have been damaged. Roads are submerged, homes are affected, traffic comes to a standstill and essential services are interrupted. Instead of asking only why rainfall is becoming extreme, we must also ask why our towns are becoming less capable of managing it. There is a tendency to treat every environmental crisis as a temporary inconvenience. A flood is discussed for a few days, a dry spring is mentioned when water tankers arrive, and an unseasonal snowfall becomes a subject of public conversation. Then attention moves elsewhere. But climate change requires long-term thinking. It cannot be addressed through occasional campaigns or official statements released after disasters. The first requirement is better environmental governance. Kashmir needs reliable, local climate data that can guide decisions in agriculture, water management, construction and disaster preparedness. Policies must be based on the specific conditions of different districts and ecological zones. What works in a high-altitude area may not work in the plains, and the needs of an orchard region may differ from those of a wetland-dependent community. The protection of forests must become a serious priority. Forests regulate water, reduce soil erosion, support biodiversity and provide protection against landslides. But forests are frequently threatened by illegal felling, fires, unplanned development and excessive human pressure. Afforestation programmes cannot simply mean planting trees and counting them. The survival of planted trees, the restoration of native species and the involvement of local communities are equally important. Traditional water systems also deserve greater attention. Springs, ponds, canals and village water channels have supported communities for generations. Many of them are now neglected, polluted or blocked. Restoring these systems can improve water security while reducing dependence on expensive emergency arrangements. Local communities should be treated as partners in conservation, not merely as beneficiaries of government schemes. The tourism sector must also examine its environmental footprint. Tourism is important for Kashmir’s economy, but uncontrolled tourism can place enormous pressure on water, waste management, roads and fragile landscapes. The answer is not to oppose visitors. It is to promote responsible tourism. Hotels and businesses must manage waste properly, conserve water and follow construction norms. Visitors, too, should understand that the valley is not an unlimited resource. Climate-conscious development does not mean stopping progress. It means redefining progress. A road that destroys a water channel is not successful development. A building constructed on a floodplain is not a sign of modernisation. A tourism project that creates waste without providing treatment facilities may generate short-term income, but it creates long-term public costs. Education has an important role in this transition. Climate change should not be taught only as a chapter in a textbook. Students should understand how it affects their own communities, farms, forests and water sources. Schools and colleges can promote rainwater harvesting, waste reduction, tree care and local biodiversity projects. Young people must be encouraged to see environmental protection not as a separate activity, but as part of responsible citizenship. The media also has a responsibility. Environmental reporting should not begin and end with disasters. It must examine the causes behind flooding, water scarcity, deforestation and pollution. It should give space to farmers, scientists, local communities and conservation workers. Public discussion becomes meaningful only when environmental issues are treated as matters of governance and justice rather than seasonal news. The administration, for its part, must move from reaction to preparedness. Early-warning systems, stronger drainage networks, safer construction practices and district-level disaster plans can save lives and reduce losses. Climate adaptation should be built into every major infrastructure project. It is cheaper and wiser to prevent damage than to repeatedly spend public money repairing the same failures. At the household level, people also have responsibilities. Waste should not be thrown into streams or drains. Water must be used carefully. Local trees and wetlands should be protected. Communities can revive collective traditions of maintaining springs, cleaning water channels and preparing for emergencies. Individual actions may seem small, but environmental degradation itself often begins with thousands of small acts of neglect. Kashmir’s climate crisis is a warning, but it is not a sentence of helplessness. The valley still has strong communities, rich ecological knowledge and natural systems capable of recovery. But recovery will not happen automatically. It requires political will, scientific planning and public participation. Most importantly, it requires a change in attitude. We must stop seeing nature as a backdrop to human life. The mountains are not merely scenery, rivers are not open drains, forests are not vacant land, and wetlands are not obstacles to construction. They are part of the living infrastructure that protects and sustains Kashmir. The future of Kashmir will depend on whether its development respects its ecology. The valley cannot preserve its identity while destroying the systems that created it. If the seasons continue to change and we continue to respond with indifference, the cost will be paid by farmers, workers, children and communities already living at the edge of insecurity. Climate change has already entered Kashmir. The question is whether Kashmir will now choose to confront it with seriousness. The choices made today will decide whether future generations inherit a living valley or only memories of the paradise we failed to protect. (The author is a research scholar and columnist)

stories.headline: A former IIT director’s blueprint: Tackling the student mental health crisis
stories.title: A former IIT director’s blueprint: Tackling the student mental health crisis
stories.summary: In the latest controversial incident at IIT-Bombay, the professor simply discharged his duties as a teacher. The actual reason for the unfortunate tragic death of the student needs to be investigated.How have these challenges evolved over the years?Some students at universities or institutes constitute a particularly vulnerable population when they feel burdened with academic pressure, financial stress, difficulties owing to social adjustment, transitions, challenges and friendships while pursuing higher education.Outside the IIT boundary, they are used to being held in high esteem. Despite being regarded as a socially privileged group, some students continue to experience depression in personal life. The actual reasons are many. These are but just a few of them:Also Read: Broken dreams, pressure of the IIT tag and shattered lives: 'We failed him. He didn't fail'1) Inadequate academic performance: A section of students loses interest in academics and some of them get involved in undesirable activities and habits.2) Some students and faculty members are concerned about issues related to living conditions in the hostels. Most of the hostels are overloaded, leading to a less-than-ideal living situation.3) It is common for some students to lose the habit of studying regularly, often due to burnout, a lack of clear goals, digital distractions or overwhelming workloads. When studying stops being a daily routine, procrastination takes over, making it even harder to return to a disciplined routine.The above issues are general problems of the entire IIT system. Several universities are also facing these issues. We need to take the bull by the horns and find solutions of general acceptability.Also Read: Inside Kota: Edgy students, caring crusaders & a missing safety valveAre current interventions sufficient, or do they require substantial rethinking?Some of the current interventions have had a good impact, but they are not wholly adequate. We need to go further.The counselling service must be made more effective and vibrant. It must try to make the time spent by the new students in the institute and their living conditions as comfortable and as memorable as possible. This will help the new entrants adjust to the system at the earliest so that they strive to achieve academic excellence in addition to the overall personal growth.The counselling service should have several teams comprising faculty counsellors and student guides. The role of the faculty counsellor should be to establish a close and sympathetic relation with the students that will last during their stay in the institute and beyond.We need to keep in mind that some students tackle plenty of obstacles. Some students find it more difficult to learn than others, some have social problems, including broken homes and financial stresses.A large number of students have communication problems. It is not only the language; it is the problem of expressing ideas even in their own mother tongue. A few suffer from economic problems. Some of them have lost confidence due to repeated failures. From the administrative side, we need to invent a variety of strategies to help somebody who has lost interest in learning or is failing to perform.Some students are bullied: About 10 percent of students are estimated to be bullied by students who appear more powerful than them in some way. An estimated 5 percent of first-year students face cyber-bullying.Professional counsellors are helpful. During my tenure, we appointed a few outstanding professional counsellors at IIT-Guwahati. We formed several teams. For instance, to bring about improvements in the living conditions in hostels, we encouraged young, enthusiastic faculty members to have occasional dinners/breakfast on Sundays at the hostels once a month.The system is dynamic and ever-changing; we must develop new strategies to handle this complex paradigm of governance. The system also has to create efficient tracks for receiving the complaints and grievances of students.Also Read: AI Companion Apps Gain Popularity in India Amid Mental Health FocusWhat role can academic leadership, faculty, peer networks and policymakers play in creating a more supportive ecosystem?For the all-round development of the students, a positive ecosystem is needed. An ecosystem that is positive, cheerful and full of activities. It will nurture every individual and their aspirations.Enhancing student engagement is not a small task. It takes deep passion, commitment and compassion to motivate each unique student. There are ways to initiate and immerse students more actively into the teaching-learning experience, requiring their thoughtfulness and participation. By becoming active learners, one can hope that students will demonstrate a level of engagement that wasn’t present before. We must come up with ideas to keep students motivated and engaged. Eventually, the ambience will progress towards a dynamic academia, which can effectively resist any “negativism”.Out-of-the-box ideas are needed to create an adequate "student care" system. We created something unique in the entire IIT system, a Centre for Creativity, at IIT-Guwahati. This acted as a stressbuster among the undergraduate as well as postgraduate students for three years during my tenure of six years there. The Centre for Creativity was developed to nurture the activities pertaining to performing arts.In every semester we used to run zero-credit courses (Senate approved) in the following disciplines of performing arts: (a) Indian classical dance (with a special focus on Sattriya dance form of Assam), (b) Instrumental music (violin and tabla) and (c) Hindustani vocal music.With a team of artists in residence, the institute performed collaborative tasks with some of the renowned cultural organisations of the country through thoughtful learning and careful curation. The wholehearted participation of students and their enthusiasm were remarkably visible. It is understood that different institutes will nurture different forms of the performing arts. It may extend from cinematography to puppetry; from Hindustani string instruments to a Hawaiian guitar—the idea is to provide the students with the space to joyfully express their emotions and creativity.The students have to understand that knowledge is power. However, this knowledge is not necessarily textbook knowledge. Science hobby clubs play a crucial role in such endeavours.Most importantly, students have to be trained to overcome failures. The idea is to help students fight back after any failure. The institute must appoint ombudsmen or ombudspersons for each hostel from among faculty members who can help fight frustration and encourage the students to overcome impediments with tenacity and wisdom. The BITS-system has adopted a similar concept in the form of “Mitra” or “Saathi”. It is a successful initiative.Also Read: Gen Z, mental health, and the role of techWhat practical reforms could be implemented to improve student wellbeing without compromising academic excellence?There are a few suggestions. However, all of these may not be easy to implement, but we can try a few at least.1) The graduation need not be completed in four years. The baccalaureate degree needs close to 160 credits (based on international credit system). The time limit by definition can be five years instead of four. A student can choose a lighter load in a semester if they are not ready to take on a full load. However, if any student can complete the programme in four years, they will not be stopped, rather they will be encouraged.2) Some reform in the “evaluation” component of pedagogy: Based on the opinion evolved in the departments by the faculty members at all levels, the academic senate may recommend a minimum of 40 to 50 percent components of a course as open-book components. Such components may include assignments, quizzes and partially proctored examinations too. The open-book component of evaluation may vary from department to department.3) Based on the recommendation of the departments, at least one course (subject) in each semester may be conducted in a flipped classroom (as an instructional method).4) The laboratory courses need not have any final examination. The evaluation can be conducted using a continuous system.5) Academically deficient students have to be given more chances to clear the backlogs to protect them from termination. If the institutes provide these additional chances, they help students overcome personal or academic hurdles without permanently derailing their futures.A supportive policy fosters resilience, giving students the space to learn without a fear of failure and successfully acquire knowledge.(The writer is senior professor emeritus-mechanical engineering at BITS Pilani, KK Birla Goa Campus. He was a professor at IIT-Kanpur from 1990 to 2024. He served as director of IIT-Guwahati from 2013 to 2019. Views are personal)

With a team of artists in residence, the institute performed collaborative tasks with some of the renowned cultural organisations of the country through thoughtful learning and careful curation.
The wholehearted participation of students and their enthusiasm were remarkably visible.
It is understood that different institutes will nurture different forms of the performing arts.

It may extend from cinematography to puppetry; from Hindustani string instruments to a Hawaiian guitar—the idea is to provide the students with the space to joyfully express their emotions and creativity.
The students have to understand that knowledge is power.
However, this knowledge is not necessarily textbook knowledge.
Science hobby clubs play a crucial role in such endeavours.
Most importantly, students have to be trained to overcome failures.
The idea is to help students fight back after any failure.

The institute must appoint ombudsmen or ombudspersons for each hostel from among faculty members who can help fight frustration and encourage the students to overcome impediments with tenacity and wisdom.
The BITS-system has adopted a similar concept in the form of “Mitra” or “Saathi”.
It is a successful initiative.
What practical reforms could be implemented to improve student wellbeing without compromising academic excellence?
There are a few suggestions.
However, all of these may not be easy to implement, but we can try a few at least.1) The graduation need not be completed in four years.
The baccalaureate degree needs close to 160 credits (based on international credit system).
The time limit by definition can be five years instead of four.
A student can choose a lighter load in a semester if they are not ready to take on a full load.
Such components may include assignments, quizzes and partially proctored examinations too.

The open-book component of evaluation may vary from department to department.3) Based on the recommendation of the departments, at least one course (subject) in each semester may be conducted in a flipped classroom (as an instructional method).4) The laboratory courses need not have any final examination.
The evaluation can be conducted using a continuous system.5) Academically deficient students have to be given more chances to clear the backlogs to protect them from termination.
If the institutes provide these additional chances, they help students overcome personal or academic hurdles without permanently derailing their futures.

A supportive policy fosters resilience, giving students the space to learn without a fear of failure and successfully acquire knowledge.(The writer is senior professor emeritus-mechanical engineering at BITS Pilani, KK Birla Goa Campus.
He was a professor at IIT-Kanpur from 1990 to 2024.
He served as director of IIT-Guwahati from 2013 to 2019.
Views are personal).
